after.en: The output no longer looks only at its own pixel, but at a weighted sum of its neighbours. This is filtering.

t.en: So far, each output cell has looked only at the cell in the same position in the input. This chapter changes that: when computing a cell, also look at the neighbours around it.

The simplest example is averaging. Replace a cell with the average of itself and its neighbours, and a lone bright dot gets spread out while flickering specks get smoothed away. A phone's night mode uses the same kind of trick to suppress noise.

From this chapter on, add, subtract and multiply are one part, <part-ref to="part:arith"></part-ref>: choose +, −, × or ÷ on the part. ÷ is new: a ÷ b divides each cell of a by the same cell of b. There is also a new part, the <part-ref to="part:merge"></part-ref>: it has three inputs and adds the pictures wired into them cell by cell; an empty input is skipped.
A new way of drawing, "Profile": the brightness along one row of the picture as a curve; drag on the picture to change row. Switch to it with the drawing buttons on a part or in the test area.

Your task in this level: replace each cell with the average of itself and its left and right neighbours. Look at the expected output below: the square's left and right edges gain a band of grey, but its top and bottom edges do not change.

brief.en: Replace each pixel with the average of itself and its left and right neighbours.

hint.en: You need the image shifted one pixel left, the image shifted one pixel right, and the original.
